text: Is the death penalty actually a prolife
policy position? Hey everybody, I'm Dan
Mlullen. I'm a scholar of the Bible and
religion. And yesterday, a person who
runs prolife advocacy groups posted this
on Twitter. Kristen Hawkins said, "The
death penalty is inconsistent with a
prolife worldview." And even the Pope
has said this. But here in this tweet,
you can see there are proposed community
notes that are disagreeing fervently
with Kristen. And you can see she's
getting ratioed in the comments as well.
And it's all the usual suspects when it
comes to Christian nationalism and
right-wing authoritarianism on the
internet. And the overwhelming majority
of the people I have seen disagreeing
with Kristen have cited a single passage
as their proof text for why the death
penalty is not only okay but is firmly
pro-life. And that passage is Genesis
9:6, which says, "Whoever sheds the
blood of a human by a human shall that
person's blood be shed. For in his own
image, God made humans." And this is the
rational foundation for what's called
Lexalionus or the Talionic law, which is
sometimes known today as retributive
justice. This is not justice aimed at
rehabilitation or at deterrence. It is
justice aimed at retribution or
vengeance, which in and of itself ought
to indicate this is probably not a very
Christ centered position. But here is
one of the clearest outlines of what
this means. If any harm follows, then
you shall give life for life, eye for
eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand,
foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for
wound, stripe for stripe. This is the
principle of doing to the perpetrator
what they did to the victim. So the
wrong cannot be writed but the same
degree of wrong can be done to the
person who did the wrong which again is
retributive. It is about retribution. It
is about vengeance. But there are
multiple problems with the notion that
Genesis 9:6 makes the death penalty a
prolife position that Christians should
endorse. And the main one is the fact
that in the New Testament, Jesus quite
explicitly commanded his followers to
live a higher law than that. We can go
to the sermon on the mount. Matthew
5:38. You have heard that it was said,
"An eye for an eye and a tooth for a
tooth." This is the lexalionus. This is
retributive justice. But I say to you,
do not resist an evildoer. But if anyone
strikes you on the right cheek, turn the
other also. And if anyone wants to sue
you and take your shirt, give your coat
as well. And if anyone forces you to go
one mile, go also the second mile. Give
to the one who asks of you. And do not
refuse anyone who wants to borrow from
you. And you might be saying, okay,
well, that's about the non-killing
retributive justice, but Jesus didn't
say, I'm overruling life for life as
well. And no, Jesus doesn't explicitly
say that. But the rest of the New
Testament makes clear that that's what
early Christians understood. And there
are a number of things that indicate
that. For instance, when Jesus is on the
cross, he cries out, "Forgive them,
father, for they know not what they do."
Which clearly is not, "I'm an innocent
life." And they're taking it. I hope you
execute them. And it's not just Jesus
who said that because we can go to Acts
7 when Stephen is martyed. While they
were stoning Stephen, he prayed, "Lord
Jesus, receive my spirit. Then he knelt
down and cried out in a loud
voice,"Lord, do not hold this sin
against them." When he had said this, he
died. Those are two very good examples
to follow if you purport to follow
Jesus. And additionally, Jesus said that
his followers would be persecuted up to
and including being put to death. And he
told them to rejoice. He told them that
your endurance is what gives you eternal
life. He said that you need to endure
these things. At no point whatsoever did
he say, "Advocate for the death
penalty." In fact, the only time the
death penalty ever comes into view,
Jesus puts a stop to it. And we know
that early Christians felt much the same
way. In fact, you had a lot of early
Christians saying, "I would rather be
put to death myself than take the life
of my attacker." And if they thought it
was inappropriate to take the life of
someone who was threatening their own
life, then there's not really a good
logical case to make that other people
would consider it appropriate to take
the life of another person because that
person had taken another person's life.
Logically, it just doesn't make much
sense. And we see for the first few
centuries of early Christianity that
overwhelmingly Christians didn't like
the death penalty. They didn't like
capital punishment. And probably the
clearest expression of this is
Athanagoras around 177 CE who writes
that we cannot endure to see a person
put to death even justly. And then
something changes in the 4th century.
That's when Christians pivot to suddenly
being okay with the death penalty. What
could have happened when Christianity
took over the Roman Empire? Oh yeah,
they took over the Roman Empire and they
became the Roman Empire and suddenly
when the lever is in their hand, they
decided that they were okay with putting
their enemies to death. And that's
really what's going on today. People are
negotiating with the text. Any attempt
to try to extract a single unified and
consistent moral or ethical principle
from the Bible requires negotiating with
it. It requires deciding what my
priorities are, finding the passages
that fit my priorities, centering them,
giving them priority, and then
subordinating other passages to it. And
here in this example, we have people
appealing to Genesis 9:6 and
subordinating everything Jesus said to
talionic justice, to retributive
justice, to the notion that justice is
about vengeance. So there's always
negotiating going on and the negotiation
process usually reveals what your
priorities are, reveals the dogmas
you're bringing to the text. And for the
earliest Christians, what they brought
to the text was what they understood
Jesus to be teaching. That life is so
sacred that we will not take it even if
it costs us our own. And then when
Christians got imperial power, suddenly
things changed. And that's why the
people who are saying no, Genesis 9:6
says retributive justice is okay.
Therefore, the death penalty is actually
a pro-life position. It reveals their
priorities, which are not about
following Jesus, but really just about
rationalizing their own right-wing
authoritarian political positions. And
this happens when the principle is not
pro-life but pro- certain lives which is
what people are saying. I care so much
about innocent life that I'm willing to
take these other lives because I declare
that they are not innocent. If you are
the one curating the threshold of
innocent and non- innocent life and
therefore what lives can be justly taken
and what lives cannot be justly taken.
that threshold is going to move
according to your own situationally
emergent needs and circumstances. You
are going to abuse that position. And
that's what's going on right now with
the notion that the death penalty is a
pro-life position. It is a pro- some
lives position. It is anti- other lives.
It's not just a blanket pro-life
position. And again, it betrays that
you're negotiating with the text in a
way that puts right-wing
authoritarianism and the structuring of
power and values and boundaries over and
directly against what Jesus pretty
clearly said in the New Testament. And
we can even go to like James 2:13 where
he said, "Mercy overrules
judgments." And Jesus twice in the
Gospel of Matthew says to go find out
what Hosea 66 means. I will have mercy
and not sacrifice. The New Testament is
pretty clear about this. And folks who
are trying to leverage Genesis 9:6 to
overrule what's going on in the New
Testament are not going to have a hard
time convincing themselves that what
they're doing is just. But they are just
negotiating in light of their own
identity politics. They're just
structuring power and values to serve
their own interests. That is precisely
the praying on the street corner that
Jesus condemned. And those folks need to
do so much better. And the fit for this
